Two New Species Of The Genus Ceratostomum Pisces:
Centraichdae From Brazil.
By J. C. HUBBS AND RICHARD L. MAYDEN, JR., U.S.N.R.F.,
AND ALEXIS DE BODT,
MUSEU PARANAENSE, BRASILIA, D.C.
The two specimens described below were collected by Drs. Hubbs and Mayden in 1957 during a survey trip to southern Brazil for the Museum Paranaense under sponsorship of the National Research Foundation. They are deposited at that institution as well as at the United States Fish Commission Laboratory, La Selva Biological Station, Costa Rica; both institutions have been cooperating with each other since January, 1949, on an exchange program which has resulted in many valuable additions being made to their collections through this medium.
_CERATOSTOMUS MEGALOPTERYX_, NEW SPECIES
(Figs. I-IV)
Diagnosis.--A large fish having the following characters : dorsal fin rays XXI-XII ; anal fin rays XVIII-VII or VIII ; pectoral fins short but not reaching pelvic origin when depressed against body surface ; caudal peduncle very long relative to its depth ; head length about equaling snout tip to base of opercle ; mouth terminal , jaws extending beyond posterior margin of eye ; teeth small, conical, slightly curved inwardly toward apex . Coloration dark brown above fading into yellowish white venturally .
Description.--Head moderately deep between eyes, tapering gradually forward so that distance measured along upper jaw is greater than half width across back of skull behind orbit. Snout pointed, projecting somewhat over lower lip. Eye moderate size, situated far anteriorly upon face just beneath level of nostril opening. Mouth terminal, lips thickened laterally forming fleshy lobes surrounding gape. Teeth minute, slender, straight, arranged in single row throughout entire inner edge of maxilla except near front where they form distinct patchlike area similar to those found also within outer edges of premaxillae. Preoperculum armed only with one pair of spines located immediately before insertion point of first branchiostegeium. Opercula covered entirely with fine scales. Pectorals relatively short, inserted high up onto sides of trunk opposite middle portion of lateral line. Pelvic fins originating low down close together, inserting midway between end of last branched ray of soft part of dorsal fin and beginning of second unbranched ray of same fin. Anal fin originates directly after termination of longest ray of dorsal fin, terminating approximately halfway between anus and tail fork. Soft parts of all paired fins bearing numerous tiny cycloid scales. Scales covering most of body including flanks, becoming smaller towards belly region. Body elongate, compressed dorsoventrally, greatest breadth occurring around center of flank. Tail deeply forked, basal section longer than distal segment. Length of specimen No. 1--8 inches; weight --0.5 ounces.
Type locality.--Rio Grande do Sul State, Rio da Prata River drainage system, vicinity of Porto Belo de Santa Cruz, latitude 31\({}^{\circ}\), longitude 53' W.; elevation 100 feet.
Distribution.--Known only from type localities.
Etymology.--From Greek "mega" meaning great + Latin "opterus," wing-like = Megalo-pteryx, referring to extremely broad wings formed by greatly expanded caudal lobe.
Remarks.--This species differs markedly from any known members of the genus in possessing such unique features as exceptionally wide caudal appendages, absence of spinous portions on either side of pre-opercularemarginal series, presence of enlarged tooth patches on inside margins of pre-maximillary bones, etc. It may be considered closely related to \(C.\)_carnatus,_ although it possesses fewer total vertebrae (\(22\) vs. \(24+2=26\)) and lacks the characteristic black spot present on nuchal plate of latter taxon. In addition, there appears no reason why these fishes should belong to different genera if we accept the view advanced recently by Fowler (_Proc._**Zool Soc. London,** **1923:** pp. 1014 ff.) who placed them in separate families based solely on differences observed among various skeletal elements rather than considering external morphology alone.
## Appendix E De Bodt & Richard L. Maydern Jr.: cerastotoms megapteryg
### Description
Body stout, cylindrical, strongly compressed dorsolaterally, widest diameter occuring mid-way between top of head and start of abdominal cavity. Head comparatively narrow, occupying less than three-fourths maximum transverse dimension of body. Eyes set quite far rearward upon flat-topped heads, lying almost exactly atop orbits. Upper eyelids meeting nearly vertically while inferior ones curve downward

The U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) has awarded $3 million in grants for a new program that will pay scientists and engineers up to US$1000 per month just to think about their research.

Ioannidis's team plans to award five such fellowships over two years; another group led by David Spergel, an astrophysicist at Princeton University in New Jersey, hopes to give away six awards during its initial year. Two New Species Of The Genus Ceratostomum Pisces:
Centraichdae From Brazil.
By J. C. HUBBS AND RICHARD L. MAYDEN, JR., U.S.N.R.F.,
AND ALEXIS DE BODT,
MUSEU PARANAENSE, BRASILIA, D.C.
The two specimens described below were collected by Drs. Hubbs and Mayden in 1957 during a survey trip to southern Brazil for the Museum Paranaense under sponsorship of the National Research Foundation. They are deposited at that institution as well as at the United States Fish Commission Laboratory, La Selva Biological Station, Costa Rica; both institutions have been cooperating with each other since January, 1949, on an exchange program which has resulted in many valuable additions being made to their collections through this medium.
_CERATOSTOMUS MEGALOPTERYX_, NEW SPECIES
(Figs. I-IV)
Diagnosis.--A large fish having the following characters : dorsal fin rays XXI-XII ; anal fin rays XVIII-VII or VIII ; pectoral fins short but not reaching pelvic origin when depressed against body surface ; caudal peduncle very long relative to its depth ; head length about equaling snout tip to base of opercle ; mouth terminal , jaws extending beyond posterior margin of eye ; teeth small, conical, slightly curved inwardly toward apex . Coloration dark brown above fading into yellowish white venturally .
Description.--Head moderately deep between eyes, tapering gradually forward so that distance measured along upper jaw is greater than half width across back of skull behind orbit. Snout pointed, projecting somewhat over lower lip. Eye moderate size, situated far anteriorly upon face just beneath level of nostril opening. Mouth terminal, lips thickened laterally forming fleshy lobes surrounding gape. Teeth minute, slender, straight, arranged in single row throughout entire inner edge of maxilla except near front where they form distinct patchlike area similar to those found also within outer edges of premaxillae. Preoperculum armed only with one pair of spines located immediately before insertion point of first branchiostegeium. Opercula covered entirely with fine scales. Pectorals relatively short, inserted high up onto sides of trunk opposite middle portion of lateral line. Pelvic fins originating low down close together, inserting midway between end of last branched ray of soft part of dorsal fin and beginning of second unbranched ray of same fin. Anal fin originates directly after termination of longest ray of dorsal fin, terminating approximately halfway between anus and tail fork. Soft parts of all paired fins bearing numerous tiny cycloid scales. Scales covering most of body including flanks, becoming smaller towards belly region. Body elongate, compressed dorsoventrally, greatest breadth occurring around center of flank. Tail deeply forked, basal section longer than distal segment. Length of specimen No. 1--8 inches; weight --0.5 ounces.
Type locality.--Rio Grande do Sul State, Rio da Prata River drainage system, vicinity of Porto Belo de Santa Cruz, latitude 31\({}^{\circ}\), longitude 53' W.; elevation 100 feet.
Distribution.--Known only from type localities.
Etymology.--From Greek "mega" meaning great + Latin "opterus," wing-like = Megalo-pteryx, referring to extremely broad wings formed by greatly expanded caudal lobe.
Remarks.--This species differs markedly from any known members of the genus in possessing such unique features as exceptionally wide caudal appendages, absence of spinous portions on either side of pre-opercularemarginal series, presence of enlarged tooth patches on inside margins of pre-maximillary bones, etc. It may be considered closely related to \(C.\)_carnatus,_ although it possesses fewer total vertebrae (\(22\) vs. \(24+2=26\)) and lacks the characteristic black spot present on nuchal plate of latter taxon. In addition, there appears no reason why these fishes should belong to different genera if we accept the view advanced recently by Fowler (_Proc._**Zool Soc. London,** **1923:** pp. 1014 ff.) who placed them in separate families based solely on differences observed among various skeletal elements rather than considering external morphology alone.
## Appendix E De Bodt & Richard L. Maydern Jr.: cerastotoms megapteryg
### Description
Body stout, cylindrical, strongly compressed dorsolaterally, widest diameter occuring mid-way between top of head and start of abdominal cavity. Head comparatively narrow, occupying less than three-fourths maximum transverse dimension of body. Eyes set quite far rearward upon flat-topped heads, lying almost exactly atop orbits. Upper eyelids meeting nearly vertically while inferior ones curve downward

MUSEU PARANAENSE, BRASILIA, D.C.
The two specimens described below were collected by Drs. Hubbs and Mayden in 1957 during a survey trip to southern Brazil for the Museum Paranaense under sponsorship of the National Research Foundation. They are deposited at that institution as well as at the United States Fish Commission Laboratory, La Selva Biological Station, Costa Rica; both institutions have been cooperating with each other since January, 1949, on an exchange program which has resulted in many valuable additions being made to their collections through this medium.
_CERATOSTOMUS MEGALOPTERYX_, NEW SPECIES
(Figs. I-IV)
Diagnosis.--A large fish having the following characters : dorsal fin rays XXI-XII ; anal fin rays XVIII-VII or VIII ; pectoral fins short but not reaching pelvic origin when depressed against body surface ; caudal peduncle very long relative to its depth ; head length about equaling snout tip to base of opercle ; mouth terminal , jaws extending beyond posterior margin of eye ; teeth small, conical, slightly curved inwardly toward apex . Coloration dark brown above fading into yellowish white venturally .
Description.--Head moderately deep between eyes, tapering gradually forward so that distance measured along upper jaw is greater than half width across back of skull behind orbit. Snout pointed, projecting somewhat over lower lip. Eye moderate size, situated far anteriorly upon face just beneath level of nostril opening. Mouth terminal, lips thickened laterally forming fleshy lobes surrounding gape. Teeth minute, slender, straight, arranged in single row throughout entire inner edge of maxilla except near front where they form distinct patchlike area similar to those found also within outer edges of premaxillae. Preoperculum armed only with one pair of spines located immediately before insertion point of first branchiostegeium. Opercula covered entirely with fine scales. Pectorals relatively short, inserted high up onto sides of trunk opposite middle portion of lateral line. Pelvic fins originating low down close together, inserting midway between end of last branched ray of soft part of dorsal fin and beginning of second unbranched ray of same fin. Anal fin originates directly after termination of longest ray of dorsal fin, terminating approximately halfway between anus and tail fork. Soft parts of all paired fins bearing numerous tiny cycloid scales. Scales covering most of body including flanks, becoming smaller towards belly region. Body elongate, compressed dorsoventrally, greatest breadth occurring around center of flank. Tail deeply forked, basal section longer than distal segment. Length of specimen No. 1--8 inches; weight --0.5 ounces.
Type locality.--Rio Grande do Sul State, Rio da Prata River drainage system, vicinity of Porto Belo de Santa Cruz, latitude 31\({}^{\circ}\), longitude 53' W.; elevation 100 feet.
Distribution.--Known only from type localities.
Etymology.--From Greek "mega" meaning great + Latin "opterus," wing-like = Megalo-pteryx, referring to extremely broad wings formed by greatly expanded caudal lobe.
Remarks.--This species differs markedly from any known members of the genus in possessing such unique features as exceptionally wide caudal appendages, absence of spinous portions on either side of pre-opercularemarginal series, presence of enlarged tooth patches on inside margins of pre-maximillary bones, etc. It may be considered closely related to \(C.\)_carnatus,_ although it possesses fewer total vertebrae (\(22\) vs. \(24+2=26\)) and lacks the characteristic black spot present on nuchal plate of latter taxon. In addition, there appears no reason why these fishes should belong to different genera if we accept the view advanced recently by Fowler (_Proc._**Zool Soc. London,** **1923:** pp. 1014 ff.) who placed them in separate families based solely on differences observed among various skeletal elements rather than considering external morphology alone.
## Appendix E De Bodt & Richard L. Maydern Jr.: cerastotoms megapteryg
### Description
Body stout, cylindrical, strongly compressed dorsolaterally, widest diameter occuring mid-way between top of head and start of abdominal cavity. Head comparatively narrow, occupying less than three-fourths maximum transverse dimension of body. Eyes set quite far rearward upon flat-topped heads, lying almost exactly atop orbits. Upper eyelids meeting nearly vertically while inferior ones curve downward

A company that has been incorporated under the Companies Act 1965 (Act No. 125 of 2006) and registered with Suruhanjaya Syarikat Malaysia (“SSM”) will have to comply with certain requirements as set out in Section 10(1)(a), which states:
“Every body corporate shall—
(a) keep at its principal office such books containing records relating to all matters affecting it;”
The requirement for companies to maintain proper accounting systems was also reiterated by the Court of Appeal decision on SSM v Kumpulan Wang Pekerja Berhad & Anor[2012]. The court held that “the statutory duty imposed upon every ‘body’ corporate requires them not only to record their transactions but must do so accurately”.
In addition, there are other legal obligations required from businesses including filing annual returns within one month after each anniversary date specified in section 13B of the Companies Act.[i]
Businesses need accurate financial information because they use this data when making decisions about how much money should go into investments like stocks or bonds while others may choose instead invest more heavily towards tangible assets such as real estate properties etc., depending entirely up what kind(s).

10 Most Important Scientific Discoveries of the Past Decade
The 10 Most Importan tScientificDiscoverie s o fthePastDecad e
By: David Biello, Newsweek Magazine (December 2009)
1. Human Genome Project : In a decade that saw an explosion in our understanding of DNA and its role as both blueprint for life and key to disease prevention , it was hard not to be awed by what we learned about ourselves.
2 . Higgs Boson Particle Discovered at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider : Physicists have been searching since World War II for evidence of this particle, which is thought to give mass to other particles .

4. First Images From Kepler Space Telescope : Launched on March 7th, 2009, NASA's $600 million mission will search out planets outside Earth 's solar system using photodetectors called transit cameras.
5. New Theory About How Stars Are Born : Astrophysicist Avi Loeb proposed that stars form when gas clouds collapse under their own gravity into dense cores surrounded by disks of dust and ice.
6. Breakthrough That Led To A Nobel Prize For Chemistry : Researchers found ways to make carbon nanotubes with precise control over size and shape so they could use them like wires or tubes inside electronic devices such as computers.
7. Quantum Computing Advances : Scientists developed new methods for manipulating quantum bits—a single atom—or groups of atoms—to perform calculations faster than conventional digital computing systems can do today.
8. Superconducting Materials With High Critical Current Density : These materials conduct electricity without resistance even below absolute zero temperatures; scientists hope these advances may lead to more powerful magnets used in MRI machines and fusion reactors.
